summary: Source-backed expansion: 5 new plants, 5 new fungi; includes African Khoi/San rooibos heritage, Ayurvedic/TCM/European/North American cultural medicine, food safety, conservation, authentic Fuling taxonomy, and 4 PubChem 2D chemical identity references. Deliberately no fabricated safe dosage or assumed polysaccharide single structure.

organisms.geographic_context: Native across parts of Europe, West/Central Asia and North Africa; European traditional herbal medicine
organisms.part_and_preparation_note: Root mucilage in described teas or other oral herbal products. Root is not interchangeable with marshmallow confectionery.

organisms.geographic_context: Western Mediterranean origin; European herbalism and ornamental/food culture
organisms.part_and_preparation_note: Flower heads in topical and oromucosal products. Plant species and extraction solvent matter.

organisms.geographic_context: Indigenous to Cape Provinces, South Africa; publicly documented Khoi and San traditional knowledge with legally acknowledged benefit sharing
organisms.part_and_preparation_note: Tea produced from aerial parts; oxidized red rooibos and unoxidized green rooibos differ chemically.

organisms.geographic_context: Indian subcontinent origin; Ayurveda and Chinese traditional medicine; grown elsewhere in Asia
organisms.part_and_preparation_note: Leaves/aerial parts as herbal preparations. Not equivalent to andrographolide injections or synthetic derivatives.

organisms.geographic_context: Central and eastern North America; historically used by several Indigenous peoples, now cultivated worldwide
organisms.part_and_preparation_note: Root, flowering aerial parts, pressed juice and concentrated extracts are different preparations; do not substitute other Echinacea species.

organisms.scientific_name: Auricularia heimuer F. Wu, B.K. Cui & Y.C. Dai
organisms.geographic_context: East Asia and commercial cultivation; taxonomically distinct from European Auricularia auricula-judae
organisms.part_and_preparation_note: Cultivated edible basidiocarps; literature for generic wood ear must not automatically be assigned to A. heimuer.

organisms.geographic_context: East Asia; cultivated edible mushroom in Japanese, Chinese and Korean food
organisms.part_and_preparation_note: Cooked fruiting bodies; the East Asian species is distinct from European Flammulina velutipes.

organisms.geographic_context: Cosmopolitan wood-decay basidiomycete; documented as a food in parts of Southeast Asia and in Philippines ethnomycology
organisms.part_and_preparation_note: Species-level culture and exposure route matter: a food preparation is not a sterile polysaccharide or a safe fungal exposure.

organisms.scientific_name: Ophiocordyceps sinensis (Berk.) G.H. Sung et al.
organisms.geographic_context: Tibetan Plateau and Himalayan alpine systems; Tibetan, Himalayan and Chinese medicinal history
organisms.part_and_preparation_note: Fungal stroma plus moth larval host from wild harvest; not interchangeable with farmed Cordyceps militaris or mycelial substitutes.

organisms.scientific_name: Pachyma hoelen Fr. (also proposed Wolfiporia hoelen)
organisms.geographic_context: East Asian cultivated medicinal sclerotium; phylogenetic studies separate it from North American Pachyma cocos (often called Wolfiporia cocos)
organisms.part_and_preparation_note: Dried subterranean sclerotium; older research labeled Poria cocos/Wolfiporia cocos may mix species. Require authentication for chemical transfers.

safety.alert: Traditional mucilage preparations may delay absorption of concurrently taken oral medicines; data for specific products and vulnerable groups are limited. Do not assume a safe dose for all ages.
Allergy can occur with Asteraceae-family plants. Minor topical applications are different from ingesting extracts, oils or unidentified flowers; EMA indications are restricted.
Ordinary rooibos beverage differs from concentrated nutraceutical extracts. Human evidence for disease treatment and standardized safe extract dosing remains insufficient.

IMPORTANT: Severe allergic reactions including anaphylaxis and a fatal report prompted Australia's 2026 removal of andrographis from its listed-medicine framework. Do not equate symptom trial data with safety.
Potentially severe allergic reactions and gastrointestinal effects; caution with asthma/allergy and possibly immunosuppressants, pregnancy and children. Cold trial efficacy inconsistent.

Commercial cultivated wood ear is food, not evidence for administering fungal polysaccharides medically. Several visually similar Auricularia species require species-level authentication; avoid wild collection based on pictures.
CDC documents Listeria outbreaks linked to enoki products: cook thoroughly and avoid raw consumption, especially for pregnant, older or immunocompromised people.

Schizophyllum commune is implicated in allergic bronchopulmonary disease and sinus/respiratory infections in human case literature. Culinary reports are NOT evidence that breathing spores or self-colonizing with this fungus is safe.

Overharvesting threatens wild Himalayan populations. Species substitution, contaminants and counterfeit products are meaningful uncertainties; human safe dosing and efficacy not established by ethnomedicinal literature.
The East Asian fu ling taxon is not necessarily the North American Wolfiporia cocos used in older analyses. Misidentification undermines compound, exposure and safety extrapolation.
